transcript:
This message comes from Thumbtack.
Avoiding your unfinished home projects because you're not sure where to start?
Thumbtack knows homes, so you don't have to.
Don't know the difference between matte paint finish and satin?
Or what that clunking sound from your dryer is?
With Thumbtack, you don't have to be a home pro, you just have to hire one.
You can hire top-rated pros, see price estimates, and read reviews, all on the app.
Download today.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. CNN and MSNow say their journalists
were denied access to Chinese President Xi Jinping's arrival to the state dinner tonight.
It comes despite a federal judge's temporary ruling blocking President Trump's ban of those
outlets in Politico from the White House.
Trump's Justice Department lawyers cited national security as a reason for the move, as NPR's
Greg Myrie explains, Trump has used the rationale multiple times.
The president's critics say he does this because judges in courts tend to be extremely
deferential when a president claims national security.
We should stress that in these recent cases, Trump didn't initially invoke national security
when he took these actions.
Only when faced with legal challenges did the president and his lawyers turn to national
security as a defense.
NPR's Greg Myrie reporting clashes broke out among groups of pro- and anti-China demonstrators
across Washington, D.C. today. Chinese President Xi's visit has divided the diaspora in the
capital.
Ahead of Xi's arrival in the U.S., demonstrators critical of Xi Jinping carrying bull horns
called for him to step down.
Other protesters donned Winnie the Pooh outfits because the cartoon character has become a
satirical meme for Xi.
But hundreds of Xi Jinping supporters gathered Thursday morning to greet the leader's motorcade
as it headed to the White House.
They sang patriotic Chinese songs like this one and waved Chinese flags as Chinese embassy
officials coordinated their movements.
The same day, demonstrators advocating for Tibetan and Hong Kong and Uyghur rights and
critical of China's ruling party say they were attacked by mass Chinese men and had
their protest flags ripped away.
Emily Fang, NPR News, Washington.
An ad running on Fox News and Newsmax showing images of President Trump and calling for the
defeat of communism was paid for by U.S. taxpayers.
The 30-second spot was the result of a $14,000 ad buy, according to Ad Impact, which tracks
media spending.
Maryland Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin says it's a violation of the Hatch Act for
government employees to work on such a video.
The British took over NATO in Norfolk for the first time today in a ceremony on board
the carrier USS Nimitz.
Steve Walsh of member station WHRO reports the moment was both symbolic and practical.
British General Nick Perry officially became the first non-American to run the only operational
command in North America.
The change comes as Europeans have begun to take a larger day-to-day leadership role as
the alliance continues to reshuffle during the second Trump administration.
"What a privilege to take command and we'll continue to deter, continue to be vigilant
and continue to show that we're ready to war fight if necessary."
NATO Joint Forces Command Norfolk is in charge of the high north in the Atlantic.
Perry says he welcomes the security agreement between the U.S. and Denmark over Greenland,
which was signed this week.
That's Brian Walsh from WHRO reporting.
U.S. stock indexes ended roughly back where they started today.
This is NPR News.
A ruling to halt deportations of people to countries other than their own has thrown
a core immigration policy of the Trump administration into question, at least temporarily, and prompted
a desperate appeal to the Supreme Court.
The ruling prompted the cancellation of a flight with 70 people that was headed to three
countries.
The Trump administration says justices need to step in to "halt that chaos."
Starbucks says it plans to close 250 stores in North America later this week.
This is the second wave of store closures under CEO Brian Nickel and NPR's Alina Seljuk reports.
In a notice to employees, Starbucks did not say how many stores it's closing in the U.S.
versus Canada or how many of the stores are unionized.
The company says affected employees would be transferred or offered severance.
CEO Brian Nickel has been trying to cut $2 billion in annual costs by 2028.
Last year, he closed more than 600 stores and cut more than 1,000 corporate jobs.
All this is funding his turnaround plan, updating the menu, speeding up service, and renovating
some locations, adding sofas and reusable mugs, trying to get people to spend more time
at the Starbucks cafes.
And the plan is showing results with customer visits and sales growing, but costs continue
to eat away at profits.
Alina Seljuk, NPR News.
Dolly Parton's last recording will appear on U2's new album.
The album "Carnival De Luz" is set to be released on November 13.
Its final track, "Torn," is a duet between Dolly and singer Bono.
Bono told Rolling Stone that the song was recorded in June just two months before Parton
died at 80 after a brief battle with cancer.
This is NPR News.
